categories.justification: The output answers the actual decision: it picks a design and lays out rollout steps. It covers every mustFlag item (alert noise, follow-the-sun, works council, DST and 5-vs-4 fairness) and also handoffs, skills coverage, cost and German working-time law. The legal detail is long, but it bears directly on what could block the rollout.
quotes: Step 1: remove alert noise first, as a precondition for any schedule change.
Both options change the Berlin on-call plan, so both need works council agreement before anything changes, pilots included.
It is 8 hours for about 28 days a year (8-29 March and 25 October to 1 November in 2026)

categories.justification: All the numbers I checked are correct: 540 pages, 335 (62%) from the three noisy alerts, 2 of them actioned, about 42 pages a week now and about 15.9 after tuning. The 2026 DST dates and the time-zone conversions are also right. Legal points that rest on background knowledge are marked HYPOTHETICAL or unverified rather than stated as fact.
quotes: three alerts (disk-usage-warning-80pct, queue-lag-warning, cert-check-flap) produce 335 of 540 pages (about 62%) and only 2 of the 173 actions
about 2.3 pages a day (about 15.9 a week; about 1.1 per 12-hour shift instead of 3, on an even spread)
ArbZG s.3 (content not retrieved in this run; from general background knowledge only)

categories.justification: It explains why each option does or does not cut night pages. It quantifies workload per person (out-of-hours, night and weekend hours) for both options and analyses edge cases specific to this case: DST weeks, where the handoff overlap goes, Berlin rest restarts, and Sunday and holiday call-outs.
quotes: Night interruptions = (pages that land in someone's local night) x (people exposed).
if the 30-minute overlap is added to the outgoing SF shift, SF runs to 22:30, or 23:30 in mismatch weeks
Splitting a fixed 168 h a week across unequal headcounts (4 vs 5) concentrates hours on the smaller office.

categories.justification: It rejects the two-option framing, questions the unverified 58% night figure, compares the options fairly with tuning applied to both, takes on strong counterarguments, and lists what would change the conclusion.
quotes: Alert-noise removal is a stronger first lever than either schedule, and it applies to both.
Unverified. It is a free-text annotation with no timestamps, and 58% of 540 is 313.2, not a whole number.
Post-tuning page volume measured over 2-4 weeks. If residual night load is negligible, a schedule change may be unnecessary.

categories.justification: The bottom line is clear: tune alerts first, then pilot follow-the-sun once the works council approves. The rollout steps are concrete and sequenced, with success and rollback criteria set in advance, a fallback, and named data to settle the open questions.
quotes: Rollout step 6: set success and rollback criteria in advance.
This is a credible fallback if the works council, legal review or skills audit blocks follow-the-sun.
Do not adopt option (a) as the main fix.

categories.justification: The structure is good and traceability is excellent: an evidence registry, recomputed calculations and labelled uncertainty. But the verdict is one very dense block of several hundred words that is hard to read, so I chose the lower anchor.
quotes: The out-of-hours figures (K25-K31, K37-K40) assume 09:00-17:00 weekday working hours in both offices. That assumption is not in the packet.

mustFlagAdjudication.quote: The three noise alerts produce 335 of 540 pages (62.0%) with 2 actions (0.6% actionable).
only after the works council has agreed, run a time-boxed pilot of follow-the-sun 12-hour shifts
Any change to the Berlin on-call plan, whether a secondary role, 12-hour shifts or a time-boxed pilot of either, needs works council agreement before it takes effect.
Berlin carries about 12% more out-of-hours hours per person than SF, and 25% more total hours (K14, K29)... about 28 days a year of DST drift

notesForHumanAdjudicator: The output's shift split (Berlin 07:00-19:00, SF 10:00-22:00 PT) differs from the reference's (Berlin about 05:00-17:00). The output's reason is to keep Berlin out of the ArbZG night window of 23:00-06:00, and it names the reference's split as the alternative. I judged this a defensible refinement, not an error. N1 (recommending option a) was not triggered: the output says 'Do not adopt option (a) as the main fix.' Both numeric targets match: V1 is about 42 pages a week and V2 is about 15.9. The only deduction is clarity, for the very dense verdict paragraph.
